facts: NBS Circular 592 reports that molybdenum-bearing stainless-steel types 316 and 317 were the most resistant to sulfuric acid at low temperatures.
The Circular states that at about 150°F all of the stainless steels corrode in practically all concentrations of sulfuric acid up to 95 percent.
Roach and Hall reported that molybdenum-bearing stainless steels were useful, at room temperature, in concentrations of sulfuric acid below 15 percent and above 85 percent.
The Circular states that resistance to sulfuric acid is improved in some cases by additions of copper or cerium.
Halide ions (for example chlorides) attack the passive film on stainless steel and produce pitting corrosion; additions of molybdenum reduce the susceptibility to pitting corrosion.

Stress-corrosion cracking severity depends on composition, corrosive medium, temperature, nature and extent of tensile stresses, and other factors; the Circular gives examples (e.g., boiling magnesium chloride produced cracks in hours while exposure to a glucose solution required 14 years).

Because the Circular ties the 316/317 advantage to low temperatures and lists multiple temperature-, concentration-, environment-, and stress-dependent limits, it does not support treating the 316/317 statement as a universal material recommendation for sulfuric-acid service.
